question: How many hours of approved continuing education must a Pennsylvania producer complete for each two-year license period?
explanation: Section 608-A(b)(1) of the Insurance Department Act of 1921 requires 24 credit hours of approved continuing education for each two-year license period as a condition of renewal. Twelve hours is a common figure in other states, not Pennsylvania's.

question: Of a Pennsylvania producer's required continuing education hours, how many must be on the topic of ethics?
explanation: Act 142 of 2024 amended section 608-A(b)(2) so that at least 3 of the 24 required hours must be on ethics. Producers who hold a property and casualty line must also complete 2 hours on flood insurance.

question: A producer completed 40 approved continuing education hours in one license period. How many hours can she carry forward to the next period?
explanation: Section 608-A(b)(1) lets excess hours carry forward to the next period, up to a maximum of 24. She has 40 - 24 = 16 excess hours, which is under the cap, so all 16 carry forward.

question: A producer's license lapsed for missing continuing education. She files the renewal form, fee and proof of the hours 45 days later. The license is reinstated:
explanation: Under section 608-A(d), a complete reinstatement request received within 60 days after the lapse is reinstated retroactively to the date the license lapsed. After 60 days reinstatement is only prospective, and after one year the person must reapply.

question: After a producer's death, the department issues his spouse a temporary license to run the agency until it is sold. The temporary license may last no more than:
explanation: Section 609-A lets the department issue a temporary license to a surviving spouse or personal representative to operate the business until it is sold, the licensee returns or new staff are licensed. It may not exceed 180 days and is not transferable.

question: A Pennsylvania producer moves and gets a new email address. She must notify the Insurance Department within:
explanation: Failing to notify the department of a change of address, telephone number or email address within 30 days is a prohibited act under section 611-A(19). Waiting until renewal would violate it.

question: A licensed producer is charged with a crime. When must he report the charges to the Insurance Department?
explanation: Section 678-A(b) requires a licensee to report criminal charges within 30 days of being charged, then to send the complaint, any pretrial order and the final disposition within 30 days of their availability. Waiting for a conviction is too late.

question: A producer wants to do business as Keystone Family Insurance instead of under her own name. She must:
explanation: Section 607-A(1) issues a license only in the licensee's own name and requires written notice to the commissioner before a fictitious name is used. Insurer approval or a county filing does not satisfy that duty.

question: Which applicant for a Pennsylvania life and accident and health license is exempt from the licensing exam?
optionA: A holder of the CLU designation
optionB: A holder of a college degree
explanation: Section 604-A(d)(2) waives the exam for a Chartered Life Underwriter applying for the life or accident and health line; CPCU and CIC holders have similar waivers for their lines. A degree, prior employment or a course alone does not exempt anyone.

question: Under current Pennsylvania law, what must an individual do before applying for a resident producer license?
explanation: Act 142 of 2024 deleted the preexamination education requirement from section 604-A, so a candidate now only has to pass the exam for the lines sought before applying. Appointments are made by insurers after the license is issued.

question: An insurer terminates a producer's appointment. It must notify the Insurance Department within:
explanation: Section 671.1-A(a) requires the insurer to notify the department within 30 days after the termination takes effect. If the reason was a violation of the act, it must say so and mail the producer a copy within 15 days.

question: Under Pennsylvania's 2024 rebating law, which of these may a producer give a personal lines customer?
optionA: A noncash gift not tied to buying
optionB: Part of the commission in cash
optionC: A gift card paid on purchase
optionD: A discount not in the policy
explanation: 40 Pa.C.S. Chapter 51 (Act 62 of 2024) still bans rebates and inducements not specified in the policy, but section 5102(c) allows noncash gifts, items or services up to an annual limit ($125 unless raised by the commissioner) if they are not contingent on a purchase. Cash back from the commission remains a prohibited rebate.

question: A producer's flyer promises a free accident policy to anyone who buys a life policy. Under Pennsylvania law this is:
optionA: Allowed if the gift is disclosed
explanation: 40 Pa.C.S. 5103 bars offering insurance as an inducement to buy another policy and using words such as free or no cost in an advertisement. The noncash gift allowance in section 5102(c) does not cover giving away insurance.

question: A producer pays an unlicensed hairdresser for referring clients who want life insurance. This is permitted only if the hairdresser:
optionC: Gets a one-time nominal flat fee
optionD: Is paid only when a policy sells
explanation: Section 672-A(b)(2) allows a fee to an unlicensed person for referrals only if the person does not discuss specific policy terms and, for personal insurance, receives no more than a one-time nominal fixed fee per referral that does not depend on a sale. Sharing commission with an unlicensed person is prohibited.

question: A Pennsylvania producer wants to charge clients $25 for filling out a life insurance application. Under state law the producer:
optionB: May, if the fee is reasonable
optionD: May not charge this fee at all
explanation: Section 674-A(b) bars any producer from charging a fee for completing an application. Fees in addition to commission are allowed only on commercial business, disclosed in advance in writing and reasonable for the services.

question: A producer deposits premiums received for several insurers in one premium account. Under Pennsylvania law this is acceptable if:
optionA: Her books show each insurer's funds
optionB: Each check is deposited the same day
optionC: All the insurers sign one agreement
optionD: The account pays the insurers interest
explanation: Section 696-A makes the producer a fiduciary who may not mingle premiums with her own funds without the insurer's express consent, but it does not require a separate account for each insurer as long as each insurer's funds are reasonably ascertainable from her books and records.

question: A producer sells an annuity at a bank branch. Pennsylvania requires a written disclosure, at or before application, that the annuity:
explanation: Section 677-A requires a licensee selling annuities or life insurance on a financial institution's premises to disclose that the product is not a deposit, is not FDIC or federally insured, is not guaranteed by the institution and, where appropriate, may lose principal. Sales must also take place apart from the deposit area.

question: A patient knowingly sends her health insurer a bill for treatment she never received, intending to be paid for it. Under Pennsylvania's Crimes Code this is:
explanation: 18 Pa.C.S. 4117(a)(2) makes it insurance fraud to knowingly, with intent to defraud, present a claim containing false or misleading material information, and section 4117(d) grades it as a felony of the third degree. Repaying later does not undo the offense.

question: Under the McCarran-Ferguson Act of 1945, primary responsibility for regulating the business of insurance belongs to:
explanation: McCarran-Ferguson declared that state regulation of insurance is in the public interest, so each state's insurance department and commissioner license insurers and producers and enforce the insurance code. The NAIC only drafts model laws and has no enforcement power, and federal law reaches insurance only where a federal statute specifically addresses it.

question: An insurer incorporated in Bermuda wants to sell life insurance policies to residents of Pennsylvania. In Pennsylvania, this company is classified as:
explanation: An alien insurer is organized under the laws of another country. A foreign insurer is one incorporated in a different U.S. state, which is the tempting choice but applies only to companies formed within the United States.

question: An insurer incorporated in Ohio has received a certificate of authority from Pennsylvania and sells policies there. In Pennsylvania, it is considered:
explanation: A company formed in another state is foreign, and one holding a certificate of authority is admitted (authorized) to transact business in that state. Non-admitted would apply only if it lacked a certificate of authority, and it is domestic only in Ohio.

question: A producer receives a client's premium check and deposits it in her personal checking account until she has time to forward it. This is:
optionA: Acceptable if the funds are forwarded within 30 days
optionB: Commingling, a breach of fiduciary duty
explanation: Section 696-A of Pennsylvania's Insurance Department Act makes a producer a fiduciary for premiums, who may not mingle them with her own funds without the insurer's express consent; doing so is commingling and can lead to license discipline. No grace window makes depositing premiums in a personal account acceptable.

question: An agent's written contract does not mention it, but the agent collects initial premiums and delivers policies because those tasks are needed to do the job. This is:
explanation: Implied authority is authority not written in the agency contract but needed to carry out the express duties. Express authority is what the contract states in writing, and apparent authority arises when the insurer's conduct leads the public to reasonably believe the agent has authority.

question: Maria shops her client's needs among many insurers and, when placing the business, legally represents the client rather than any insurer. Maria is acting as:
explanation: A broker represents the insured or applicant, while an agent, whether captive or independent, represents the insurers that appointed him. An independent agent can also place business with many insurers, but he still legally represents those insurers, not the client.

question: A producer persuades a client to drop a whole life policy and buy a new one from a different insurer by misrepresenting the old policy's terms. This is:
explanation: Twisting is inducing a policyowner to lapse or replace a policy with another insurer's policy through misrepresentation or an incomplete comparison. Churning is similar but involves replacing policies within the same insurer, often to generate new commissions.

question: To win business, an agent tells prospects that a competing insurer is about to go bankrupt, although she knows the statement is false. This is:
explanation: Making false or maliciously critical statements about another insurer's financial condition or another producer's character is defamation. Misrepresentation, by contrast, involves false statements about the terms or benefits of a policy.

question: A producer's printed flyer calls a participating whole life policy a 'savings account' and states that its dividends are guaranteed. This is:
explanation: Misstating a policy's nature, terms or benefits, such as calling it a savings account or promising guaranteed dividends, is misrepresentation, and doing so in printed material is also false advertising. Dividends can never be guaranteed, and defamation concerns false statements about competitors, not one's own product.

question: An insurer declines a life insurance applicant based partly on information in a consumer report. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the insurer must:
optionA: Tell the applicant and name the reporting agency
optionB: Keep the consumer report secret from the applicant
optionD: Get approval from the state commissioner before declining
explanation: When adverse action is based on a consumer report, the FCRA requires the insurer to notify the applicant and identify the reporting agency so the person can get a free copy and dispute inaccurate information. The commissioner does not approve individual underwriting decisions.

question: Ray was convicted of a felony involving dishonesty years ago and now wants a job at an insurance company. Under federal law (18 USC 1033), he must first:
optionA: Wait ten years after completing his sentence
optionB: Obtain written consent from the state regulator
optionC: Obtain a pardon from the U.S. Department of Justice
optionD: Disclose the conviction to every customer he serves
explanation: Under 18 USC 1033, part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994, a person convicted of a felony involving dishonesty or breach of trust may not work in the business of insurance without written consent from the state insurance regulator. No waiting period automatically removes the bar, and the same law makes knowingly false statements to regulators a federal crime.

question: Which statement about federal privacy and telemarketing rules affecting insurance producers is accurate?
optionA: Do Not Call rules exempt all insurance telemarketing calls
optionB: GLBA bans insurers from sharing any customer data
optionC: Insurers must provide customers privacy notices
optionD: Registry numbers may be called once per calendar year
explanation: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires insurers to give privacy notices explaining their information-sharing practices and to let consumers opt out of sharing nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties. Insurance telemarketers must honor the National Do Not Call Registry, subject to limited exceptions such as an established business relationship.

question: Jake buys shares of a startup company, hoping for a large gain but knowing he could lose his entire investment. This type of risk is:
explanation: Speculative risk involves the chance of loss, gain or no change, as with investing or gambling, and is not insurable. Pure risk offers only the chance of loss or no loss, and only pure risk can be insured.

question: Since buying insurance, Tom has stopped locking his car because he figures any theft will be covered. This attitude is an example of:
explanation: Morale hazard is indifference or carelessness toward loss because insurance exists. Moral hazard is dishonesty or bad character, such as faking a claim, and a peril is the cause of loss itself, such as theft.

question: An insurer notices that people in poor health are more likely to apply for life insurance than healthy people. This tendency is called:
explanation: Adverse selection is the tendency of poorer-than-average risks to seek insurance more often, which insurers control through underwriting. Moral hazard refers to an applicant's dishonesty, not the tendency of high-risk people to buy coverage.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the elements of an insurable risk?
optionA: The loss must be due to chance
optionB: The loss must be definite and measurable
optionD: Exposure units must be numerous and similar
explanation: An insurable loss must NOT be catastrophic, because a loss striking many insureds at once, such as war, would make losses unpredictable. Chance, definite and measurable losses, and a large group of similar units are all required elements.

question: A business installs a sprinkler system and holds regular fire safety training to lower the chance and severity of a fire. This risk management method is:
explanation: Reduction lowers the likelihood or severity of a loss without eliminating the exposure. Avoidance would mean eliminating the exposure entirely, retention means accepting the loss yourself, and buying insurance is the classic example of transfer, while sharing spreads losses among a group.

question: Sandra receives a dividend check from the insurer that issued her participating whole life policy, and she can vote for its board. The insurer is most likely a:
explanation: A mutual insurer is owned by its policyholders, issues participating policies, and returns surplus as dividends that are treated as a return of premium. A stock insurer is owned by shareholders and generally issues nonparticipating policies, paying dividends to stockholders rather than policyholders.

question: Dana pays her first $400 premium and dies in an accident a week later, and her beneficiary receives $250,000. This illustrates that the policy is:
explanation: An aleatory contract involves an unequal exchange of values that depends on an uncertain event, so a small premium can buy a large benefit. Unilateral means only the insurer makes an enforceable promise, which is true but is not what the unequal exchange shows.

question: A policy provision is ambiguous, and a court interprets it in favor of the insured because the insurer wrote the contract. This reflects that the policy is a contract of:
explanation: Insurance is a contract of adhesion, offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis with wording written by the insurer, so any ambiguity is construed against the insurer. Utmost good faith refers to the honesty both parties owe each other, not to how unclear wording is read.

question: Statements an applicant makes on a life insurance application are considered true to the best of the applicant's knowledge and belief. These statements are:
explanation: Application answers are representations, true to the best of the applicant's belief, and only a material misrepresentation lets the insurer void the contract. Warranties are statements guaranteed to be literally true, where any breach could void the contract, which is why application answers are not treated as warranties.

question: An applicant knows she had a heart attack last year but intentionally withholds that fact from the insurer to obtain coverage. This is:
explanation: Concealment is intentionally withholding a known material fact, and it can void the policy within the contestable period. Misrepresentation is making a false statement, and fraud is an intentional deception meant to induce the other party to act to its harm.

question: For two years an insurer accepted late premiums without objection. When it later tries to lapse the policy over a late payment, a court prevents it. This is:
explanation: Estoppel prevents a party from reasserting a right after its own conduct led the other party to rely on it giving that right up. By accepting late premiums for two years, the insurer led the owner to rely on that practice, so a court bars the lapse. Indemnity is the principle of restoring an insured to the pre-loss condition and has nothing to do with this dispute.

question: An applicant pays the first premium with the application and gets a conditional receipt. She dies after the medical exam but before policy issue, and she was insurable. The insurer:
optionD: Denies the claim since no policy issued
explanation: Under a conditional receipt, coverage begins on the later of the application or medical exam date if the applicant proves insurable as applied for, so the claim is paid. A binding receipt, by contrast, gives temporary coverage immediately for a limited period whether or not the applicant is later found insurable.

question: No premium was paid with an application. The policy is issued on May 1 and delivered on May 10, when the producer collects the premium. Coverage begins:
explanation: With no premium at application, coverage starts only when the policy is delivered, the first premium is paid and a statement of good health is signed, which all happened on May 10. Issuing the policy on May 1 does not start coverage because the insurer had not yet received the premium.

question: An insurer's medical examiner reports an applicant as fit for insurance. Unless the report was obtained by fraud, the insurer may not later argue that the applicant:
optionA: Was in poor health at the exam
explanation: Section 411A of The Insurance Company Law of 1921 estops an insurer whose examiner certified the applicant as fit from claiming the insured was not in the required health at the time of the exam, unless the certificate was procured by the insured's fraud or misrepresentation. Nonpayment and policy exclusions remain available defenses.

question: Which of the following would NOT typically have an insurable interest in the life of the proposed insured?
optionA: A business relying on the insured as a key employee
optionB: A creditor, up to the amount of the debt
optionC: The insured's spouse of ten years
optionD: A neighbor who has known the insured for years
explanation: Insurable interest requires a financial stake or close family tie in the insured's continued life; friendship alone does not qualify. A creditor does have an insurable interest, but only up to the amount owed.

question: Dan, 40, earns $90,000 a year and spends $30,000 of it on himself. He plans to work 25 more years. Before discounting, his human life value is:
explanation: Human life value uses the earnings the family would lose: ($90,000 - $30,000) x 25 years = $1,500,000, which is then discounted to present value. $2,250,000 wrongly includes the $30,000 Dan spends on himself.

question: A family needs $20,000 for final expenses, $180,000 to pay off the mortgage and $100,000 for education. Existing group life is $50,000. Using the needs approach, how much more coverage?
explanation: The needs approach totals the obligations ($20,000 + $180,000 + $100,000 = $300,000) and subtracts existing resources ($50,000), leaving $250,000. $300,000 forgets to subtract the group coverage already in place.

question: The human life value approach to determining how much life insurance a person needs is based on:
optionA: The total of final expenses, debts and education costs
optionB: The face amount the insured can comfortably afford to pay for
optionC: The cash value needed to fund retirement at age 65
optionD: The present value of future earnings lost to the family
explanation: Human life value measures the insured's economic worth as the present value of the income the family would lose. Totaling specific obligations such as final expenses, debts and education is the needs approach.

question: Hank owns a large farm but has little cash. He worries his heirs would have to sell land to pay estate taxes and debts. Life insurance would provide:
explanation: Death proceeds give heirs cash to pay taxes and debts without a forced sale of illiquid assets, which is estate liquidity. Key person coverage protects a business from losing an employee, not an estate from a cash shortage.

question: A software firm's success depends on its lead engineer. The firm buys a policy on her life to offset lost profits and hiring costs. Who is owner and beneficiary?
optionA: The engineer owns it; the firm is beneficiary
optionB: The firm is owner, premium payer and beneficiary
optionC: The firm owns it; her family is beneficiary
optionD: The engineer owns it, and her family is the beneficiary
explanation: In key person coverage the business applies for, owns, pays for and is the beneficiary of the policy because the business suffers the loss. Naming her family as beneficiary would make it a personal benefit, not key person protection.

question: Five shareholders want a buy-sell plan in which the corporation owns one policy on each of them and redeems a deceased owner's shares. This is called:
optionA: A cross-purchase plan among the owners
optionC: A split-dollar arrangement covering each shareholder
optionD: A key person plan owned by the company
explanation: Under an entity purchase the business buys, owns and is beneficiary of a policy on each owner, then uses the proceeds to buy the deceased owner's interest. In a cross purchase the owners buy policies on each other, so the business would not own them.

question: A company pays a yearly bonus that its sales director uses to pay premiums on a policy he owns. Under Section 162, the bonus is:
optionA: Deductible to the company and tax-free to him
optionB: Not deductible to the company but tax-free to him
optionC: Not deductible to the company and taxable to him
optionD: Deductible to the company and taxable to him
explanation: In a Section 162 executive bonus plan the bonus is reasonable compensation, so the employer deducts it and the employee reports it as income. Treating it as tax-free to the employee confuses it with the first $50,000 of group term coverage under Section 79.

question: In group life insurance, who is the policyowner, and what do the covered employees receive?
optionA: Each employee owns an individual policy; the employer gets certificates
optionB: The insurer owns the policy; employees get riders
optionC: The employer owns a master policy; employees get certificates
optionD: The union owns the policy; employees get individual contracts
explanation: The employer is the policyowner of a single master contract, and each insured employee receives a certificate of insurance describing the coverage. Individual ownership by each employee is how individual, not group, insurance works.

question: Pennsylvania defines insurable interest between persons related by blood or law as an interest:
explanation: Section 412 of The Insurance Company Law defines insurable interest for relatives as an interest engendered by love and affection, and for others as a lawful economic interest in the insured's continued life. An interest that would arise only from the insured's death does not qualify.

question: A Pennsylvania corporation plans to buy life insurance on its employees. Before buying, it must:
explanation: Section 412 lets an employer insure its officers, directors, partners and employees without their personal applications only if it notifies them in writing of its intent and obtains their prior written consent. No commissioner approval is required.

question: A producer tells a client a new policy is safe because the state guaranty association would pay if the insurer failed. Under Pennsylvania law this is:
explanation: Section 1717 of The Insurance Company Law bars any member insurer, agent or affiliate from using the existence of the life and health guaranty association to sell or induce a purchase. Insurers instead deliver an approved summary document describing the association's purposes and limits.

question: An employee's group life coverage ends when he quits. Under Pennsylvania's Group Life Insurance Policy Law, he may convert without evidence of insurability if he applies and pays within:
explanation: Section 6(8) of the Group Life Insurance Policy Law requires a right to convert to an individual policy, on any form the insurer issues except term, if application and first premium are made within 31 days after termination. If he is not notified of the right at least 15 days before it expires, section 7 extends it, but never more than 60 days.

question: A former employee dies 20 days after his group life coverage ended, before applying to convert it. The group policy:
optionB: Pays the amount he could convert
optionD: Pays only if he had applied
explanation: Section 6(10) of the Group Life Insurance Policy Law requires the group policy to pay, as a claim, the amount the person could have converted if he dies within the 31-day conversion period, whether or not he applied or paid the first premium.

question: Kevin and Lisa have a 30-year, $300,000 mortgage and want coverage that shrinks as the loan balance falls. Which policy fits best?
explanation: Decreasing term has a level premium and a face amount that declines over the term, roughly matching a mortgage balance. Level term would keep paying the full $300,000 even after much of the loan is repaid, costing more than needed.

question: A renewable feature in a term life policy allows the policyowner to:
optionA: Exchange it for whole life without evidence of insurability
optionB: Renew for another term without evidence of insurability
optionC: Renew at the original issue-age premium rate
optionD: Receive premiums back if the insured survives
explanation: Renewability lets the owner extend coverage for another term without evidence of insurability, though the premium rises to the insured's attained age. Exchanging for whole life without evidence is the convertible feature, not renewability.

question: Tom bought 20-year convertible term at age 30. At 45 he is diagnosed with diabetes and wants lifelong coverage. What can he do?
optionA: Convert to whole life without evidence of insurability
optionB: Renew the term for another 20 years at the original rate
optionC: Apply for whole life with a new medical exam
optionD: Add an increasing term rider to extend the coverage
explanation: The conversion privilege lets Tom exchange term for permanent insurance without proving insurability, usually at his attained age. Applying with a new exam would expose him to a rating or decline because of the diabetes.

question: Under a straight whole life policy, when does the cash value equal the face amount?
optionA: After premiums have been paid for 20 years
optionC: At the end of the incontestable period
explanation: Straight whole life charges a level premium for life, and the cash value grows to equal the face amount when the policy endows at age 100 or 121, depending on the mortality table. Premiums stopping at 65 describes a limited pay policy.

question: Dr. Chen, 40, wants permanent coverage but wants no premiums due after she retires at 65. Which policy fits?
explanation: Limited pay whole life compresses premiums into a set period, such as to age 65, after which the policy is paid up for life. Straight whole life requires premiums for the insured's entire life.

question: A self-employed contractor with uneven income wants permanent coverage and the ability to skip or reduce premiums in lean years. Which policy fits best?
explanation: Universal life has flexible premiums: the owner can pay more, less or skip a payment as long as the cash value covers the monthly charges. Variable life has fixed, scheduled premiums.

question: A universal life owner wants the death benefit to equal the face amount plus the accumulated cash value. Which choice should she make?
explanation: Option B pays the specified face amount plus the cash value, so the death benefit increases as cash value grows. Option A keeps the death benefit level, so rising cash value only reduces the insurer's net amount at risk.

question: An agent wants to start selling variable life insurance to clients. Which licenses or registrations are required?
optionA: Life license plus a state adjuster license
optionB: FINRA securities registration with no insurance license
optionC: Life license only, since it is insurance
optionD: Life license plus FINRA securities registration
explanation: Variable products are both insurance and securities, so the agent needs a state life license and FINRA registration, such as the Series 6 or 7. A life license alone is not enough because the cash value is invested in a separate account.

question: Ana wants cash value growth linked to a stock market index but never wants a negative credit in a down year. Which policy fits?
optionA: Variable universal life with stock subaccounts
optionB: Indexed universal life with a floor
optionC: Straight whole life with annual dividends
optionD: Level term with a return of premium rider
explanation: Indexed universal life credits interest based on an index, limited by a cap and participation rate, with a floor (often 0%) that prevents losses from index declines. Variable universal life invests in subaccounts and can lose value in a down market.

question: A wealthy married couple wants a policy to pay the estate taxes due after the second spouse dies. Which policy fits best?
explanation: Survivorship life pays only at the second death, when estate taxes usually come due because of the unlimited marital deduction at the first death, and it costs less than two single policies. Joint first-to-die life pays too early, at the first death.

question: The owner of a new individual fixed-dollar life policy, not a replacement, may return it in Pennsylvania for a full premium refund within at least:
explanation: Section 410D(a)(1) of The Insurance Company Law requires a notice that the owner may return the policy within at least 10 days of delivery for a refund. Replacement policies get longer periods: 20 days from a different insurer and 45 days from the same insurer group.

question: A client replaces her life policy with one from a different insurer. Her Pennsylvania right to return the new policy for a refund lasts at least:
explanation: Section 410D(a)(3) gives at least 20 days after delivery when the policy replaces coverage with a different insurer or insurer group, and 31 Pa. Code 81.6(d) requires the same 20-day unconditional refund notice. Forty-five days applies only to a replacement within the same insurer group.

question: A policyowner replaces an existing life policy with a new policy from the same insurer group. The new policy's free-look period in Pennsylvania is at least:
explanation: Section 410D(a)(2) requires a notice allowing return within at least 45 days of delivery when the new policy replaces a life policy or annuity with the same insurer or insurer group. A replacement from a different insurer gets 20 days.

question: A Pennsylvania whole life policy lapsed for nonpayment and was not surrendered. The owner may apply for reinstatement within:
explanation: Section 410(k) requires a reinstatement provision allowing written application within three years of default, unless the policy was surrendered or the extended term expired, with evidence of insurability and overdue premiums plus interest of no more than 8% a year.

question: Under Pennsylvania law, a life policy may not take effect more than how long before the original application was made?
explanation: Section 411(c) of The Insurance Company Law prohibits a life policy provision dating the policy to take effect more than six months before the original application. Backdating saves age but cannot go further back than that.

question: An insurer receives satisfactory proof of death but pays the life claim 45 days later. Under Pennsylvania law, it must:
optionB: Pay the face amount, no interest
optionC: Pay interest from the claim date
optionD: Pay interest from the death date
explanation: Section 411B makes death benefits not paid within 30 days after satisfactory proof bear interest at the insurer's rate for proceeds left on deposit, accruing from the date of death. Only when proof arrives more than 180 days after death does interest run from the date of proof.

question: A Pennsylvania insured named his wife revocable beneficiary and never changed it. They divorced, and he dies. Absent a court order or contract saying otherwise, the policy is paid:
optionB: Equally to her and his estate
optionC: As if she had died first
explanation: Under 20 Pa.C.S. 6111.2, a revocable designation of a spouse becomes ineffective on divorce and is read as if the former spouse predeceased the insured, unless the wording, a court order, a written contract or a post-divorce designation shows it was meant to survive. The contingent beneficiary, if any, then takes.

question: Maria owns and pays for a life policy on her adult son, who is the insured. Who may change the beneficiary or take a policy loan?
explanation: Ownership rights such as naming beneficiaries, borrowing and assigning belong to the policyowner, not the insured. The insured's consent is needed at application, but not to exercise later ownership rights.

question: A $100,000 policy has a $1,200 annual premium due March 1 that goes unpaid. The insured dies March 20. The insurer will pay:
explanation: Pennsylvania requires a grace period of 30 days or one month (Insurance Company Law section 410(b)), so the policy was still in force on March 20. The insurer pays the face amount minus the overdue premium: $100,000 - $1,200 = $98,800, not the full $100,000.

question: A whole life policy lapsed for nonpayment 14 months ago, and the owner now asks to reinstate it. The insurer will typically require:
optionA: Insurability evidence and back premiums with interest
optionB: Only the missed premium, with no proof of health required
optionC: A new application priced at the original age
optionD: Repayment of the full cash value
explanation: Pennsylvania requires a reinstatement provision allowing application within three years of default (Insurance Company Law section 410(k)), with evidence of insurability and overdue premiums plus interest. Paying only the missed premium is not enough, and a surrendered policy cannot be reinstated.

question: An insured with a $250,000 whole life policy owes a $20,000 policy loan plus $1,000 of accrued interest when he dies. The beneficiary receives:
optionA: $250,000, since loans do not reduce it
explanation: Unpaid loans and interest are deducted from the death benefit: $250,000 - $20,000 - $1,000 = $229,000. Forgetting the accrued interest gives the tempting but wrong $230,000.

question: A policyowner misses a premium and the grace period ends. Her whole life policy has enough cash value and an automatic premium loan provision. What happens?
optionA: The premium is borrowed from the cash value
optionB: The policy converts to extended term
optionC: The policy lapses and must be reinstated
optionD: The policy becomes reduced paid-up insurance
explanation: The automatic premium loan provision pays the overdue premium as a loan against the cash value, keeping the policy in force. Extended term would apply only if there were no APL provision and no option chosen.

question: Three years after issue, an insured dies, and the insurer discovers he concealed a heart condition on the application. Premiums were paid. The insurer:
optionB: May deny the claim for concealment
optionC: May refund premiums instead of paying
optionD: May reduce the benefit by half
explanation: After the two-year incontestable period, the insurer cannot contest for misrepresentation or concealment. The exceptions are nonpayment of premium and, in some cases, impersonation or lack of insurable interest, none of which applies here.

question: An insured dies with a $100,000 policy. He paid $20 per $1,000, but the correct premium for his true age was $25 per $1,000. The insurer pays:
explanation: Under misstatement of age, the benefit is adjusted to what the premium paid would have bought: $2,000 paid / $25 per $1,000 = 80 units, or $80,000. The contract is not voided, and the full face is not paid.

question: Tom names his wife primary beneficiary and his two children contingent beneficiaries. His wife dies first, and Tom later dies without changing anything. Proceeds go to:
explanation: Contingent beneficiaries receive the proceeds when no primary beneficiary survives the insured. Proceeds go to the estate only if no named beneficiary survives, so probate is not involved.

question: As part of a divorce settlement, Ken named his ex-wife the irrevocable beneficiary. He now wants to name his new wife instead. He:
optionA: May change it by notifying the insurer
optionD: Must wait for the next policy anniversary
explanation: An irrevocable beneficiary has a vested interest, so the owner cannot change the designation without that beneficiary's consent. Notice alone works only for a revocable beneficiary.

question: A policyowner stops paying premiums on a whole life policy with cash value, has no automatic premium loan, and never chooses a nonforfeiture option. The insurer applies:
explanation: Extended term is the automatic option in most policies: the cash value buys term coverage for the same face amount for as long as it lasts. Reduced paid-up must be elected.

question: A retiree wants to stop paying premiums but keep permanent coverage for life, accepting a smaller face amount. Which nonforfeiture option fits?
optionA: Extended term insurance at full face
explanation: Reduced paid-up uses the cash value as a single premium for a smaller permanent policy that lasts for life. Extended term keeps the full face amount but only for a limited period.

question: An insured is diagnosed with a terminal illness and expected to live less than a year. Which rider lets her receive part of the death benefit now?
explanation: Accelerated (living) benefits pay part of the death benefit to a terminally ill insured, reducing what the beneficiary later receives. A payor benefit rider waives a juvenile policy's premiums if the payor dies or is disabled.

question: A father buys an annuity on his daughter's life and names his wife to receive any value left at death. Whose life determines the payments?
optionD: Whichever of the three is oldest
explanation: The annuitant is the person whose life expectancy measures the annuity payments. The owner controls and funds the contract, but owning it does not make the father the measuring life.

question: During which phase of a deferred annuity does the owner pay premiums while the account earns tax-deferred interest?
explanation: Premiums are paid and earnings build tax-deferred during the accumulation phase. The annuitization (payout) phase comes later, when the value is converted into a stream of income.

question: A 66-year-old retiree deposits a $200,000 lump sum and wants income to start next month. Which annuity best fits her goal?
explanation: An immediate annuity is bought with a single premium and begins payments within 12 months. A single premium deferred annuity is funded the same way but postpones income for years, which does not meet her need.

question: Which type of annuity requires the selling producer to hold both a life insurance license and a securities registration?
explanation: A variable annuity invests through the insurer's separate account in subaccounts, so it is a security and requires FINRA registration plus a life license. An indexed annuity tracks an index but guarantees principal through a floor, so a life license alone is enough.

question: Which annuity payout option provides the highest monthly income from a given amount of money?
explanation: Life only pays the most per month because payments stop at the annuitant's death and nothing goes to a beneficiary. Every option that adds a guarantee, such as a period certain or a refund, lowers the monthly amount.

question: An annuitant chose life with 10-year period certain and dies after receiving monthly payments for 4 years. What happens next?
optionA: Payments stop and the insurer keeps the balance
optionB: The beneficiary receives payments for 10 more years
optionC: The beneficiary receives payments for 6 more years
optionD: The beneficiary receives all premiums in a lump sum
explanation: The period certain guarantees 10 years of payments in total, so the beneficiary receives the remaining 6 years (10 - 4). Payments would stop at death only under a life only option.

question: A married couple wants annuity income that continues for as long as either spouse remains alive. Which payout option should they choose?
optionC: Straight life on the older spouse
explanation: Joint and survivor keeps paying until the second death, possibly at a reduced survivor amount. Joint life sounds similar but stops all payments at the first death.

question: An owner invested $60,000 in a nonqualified annuity with an expected total return of $100,000 and receives $500 monthly. How much of each payment is taxable?
explanation: The exclusion ratio is $60,000 / $100,000 = 60%, so $300 of each $500 payment is a tax-free return of cost basis. The remaining $200 is earnings taxed as ordinary income; $300 is the excluded portion, not the taxable one.

question: A client wants to move cash value to a new contract without current taxation. Which exchange does NOT qualify under Section 1035?
optionA: Life insurance policy exchanged for an annuity
optionC: Life policy exchanged for another life policy
optionD: Annuity exchanged for a life insurance policy
explanation: Section 1035 allows tax-free exchanges of life for life, life for annuity, and annuity for annuity. Moving from an annuity to life insurance is not allowed because it would convert tax-deferred gain into a tax-free death benefit.

question: A policyowner paid $40,000 in premiums and surrenders a whole life policy for its $55,000 cash value. How much is taxable?
optionC: Nothing, since cash value is tax-free
explanation: Cash value grows tax-deferred, and at surrender only the gain above cost basis ($55,000 - $40,000 = $15,000) is taxed. That gain is ordinary income, not a capital gain.

question: A policyowner pays a large single premium, and the policy fails the 7-pay test. Which consequence follows?
optionA: The death benefit becomes taxable income
optionB: Loans and withdrawals are taxed LIFO, possibly with penalty
optionC: The policy can regain non-MEC status after seven years
optionD: The cash value stops growing tax-deferred
explanation: A policy failing the 7-pay test becomes a modified endowment contract: loans and withdrawals are taxed earnings-first, with a 10% penalty before 59 1/2, while a non-MEC loan is not taxable. The death benefit stays income tax-free, and once a MEC, always a MEC.

question: A 35-year-old expects to be in a higher tax bracket in retirement and wants tax-free income then. Which account best fits?
explanation: Roth IRA contributions are made after tax, and qualified withdrawals are entirely tax-free, which helps most when future rates are higher; the owner also has no RMDs. A traditional IRA gives a deduction now but taxes withdrawals later at the higher rate.

question: A 45-year-old leaving her job takes a $50,000 401(k) distribution payable to herself, intending to roll it over. What happens?
optionA: Nothing is withheld if she redeposits within 60 days
optionD: Nothing is withheld; she has 30 days
explanation: An indirect rollover from a qualified plan triggers mandatory 20% withholding ($50,000 x 20% = $10,000), and she must redeposit within 60 days, replacing the withheld $10,000 from other funds to avoid tax on it. A direct trustee-to-trustee rollover would avoid the withholding.

question: A buyer of an individual fixed annuity in Pennsylvania, not a replacement, may return it for a full refund within at least:
explanation: Section 410E(a)(1) of The Insurance Company Law requires a notice allowing return within at least 10 days of delivery with a refund of the premium. Replacements get 20 days from a different insurer and 45 days within the same insurer group.

question: A producer recommends replacing a client's annuity. The Notice Regarding Replacement must be given to the applicant:
explanation: 31 Pa. Code 81.4(b) requires the agent, no later than taking the application, to present the Notice Regarding Replacement of Life Insurance and Annuities signed by applicant and agent, list the contracts being replaced and leave copies of the sales materials used.

question: When replacement is involved, the replacing insurer must send the existing insurer written notice of it within:
explanation: 31 Pa. Code 81.6(a)(2)(ii) requires the replacing insurer to notify each existing insurer within 5 working days of receiving the application or issuing the contract, whichever is sooner. An existing insurer that tries to conserve the business then has 20 days to send the owner a disclosure or ledger statement.

question: Health insurance policies protect against losses caused by which two perils?
explanation: Health insurance covers the perils of accident and sickness, which cause medical expenses and lost income. Premature death is the peril covered by life insurance.

question: A carpenter wants a policy that replaces part of his paycheck if an injury or illness keeps him from working. He needs:
explanation: Disability income insurance replaces a portion of earnings lost to accident or sickness. Major medical pays medical bills, not lost income.

question: An HMO member wants to see a dermatologist for a skin condition. Under a typical HMO, the member must first:
optionA: Pay the full cost, then file a claim
optionC: Choose any dermatologist, in or out of the network
optionD: Get a referral from her primary care physician
explanation: The HMO primary care physician acts as a gatekeeper, and specialist visits require a referral. HMOs usually charge copays rather than requiring members to pay in full and file claims.

question: An HMO pays each primary care physician a fixed monthly amount per enrolled member, regardless of services used. This method is called:
explanation: Capitation pays providers a set amount per member per month, giving them an incentive to keep members healthy. Fee-for-service, used by indemnity plans, pays for each service performed.

question: A PPO member sees an out-of-network specialist without any referral. How will the plan typically treat the claim?
optionB: It pays benefits, but at a lower level
optionC: It pays the same as in-network care
optionD: It requires a PCP referral before paying
explanation: PPOs allow out-of-network care without referrals, but the member pays more through higher deductibles and coinsurance. Denying out-of-network care except emergencies is typical of an HMO or EPO, not a PPO.

question: Which plan type lets members decide at each visit between gatekeeper network care and out-of-network care at higher cost?
explanation: A point-of-service plan blends HMO and PPO features: members use a primary care gatekeeper in network but may go out of network for lower benefits. An EPO generally does not cover out-of-network care at all.

question: A family wants to see any doctor or hospital with no network, paying a deductible and coinsurance. Which plan type fits?
explanation: An indemnity plan reimburses covered charges from any provider after the deductible and coinsurance, with no network. HMOs and EPOs restrict members to network providers except for emergencies.

question: Which renewability provision gives the insured the greatest protection against cancellation and premium increases?
explanation: Under a noncancelable policy the insurer can neither cancel nor raise premiums, as long as premiums are paid. Guaranteed renewable also prevents cancellation but allows class-wide premium increases.

question: An insurer raises premiums for an entire class of disability policyholders, but it cannot cancel any individual policy. These policies are:
explanation: Guaranteed renewable policies must be renewed, but premiums can rise for an entire class. A noncancelable policy would not allow any premium increase.

question: To make tax-deductible contributions to a health savings account, an individual must:
optionA: Spend the full balance by year-end
optionB: Be enrolled in Medicare Part B
optionC: Be covered by a qualified high-deductible health plan
optionD: Work for an employer that sponsors and funds the account
explanation: HSA eligibility requires HDHP coverage; contributions are deductible, growth is tax-free and qualified withdrawals are tax-free. The use-it-or-lose-it rule belongs to flexible spending accounts, and HSA balances roll over.

question: In Pennsylvania, an individual accident and sickness policy, other than a single premium nonrenewable one, must let the owner return it for a refund within:
explanation: Section 617(A)(10) of The Insurance Company Law requires a notice that the policyholder may return the policy within 10 days of delivery, after which it is void from the beginning. Medicare supplement and long-term care policies have longer 30-day periods.

question: A Pennsylvania insurer calls an individual health policy noncancellable. The law requires that policy to be:
optionA: Renewable one year at a time
explanation: Section 617(A)(8) requires a policy entitled or referred to as noncancellable to be automatically renewable until age 60 upon payment of the required premiums. Renewal at the insurer's option describes an optionally renewable policy.

question: Mary pays her individual health premium monthly, due June 1. She is hospitalized June 8 and has not yet paid. Her policy is:
optionA: Lapsed, because the grace period for monthly premiums is 7 days
optionB: Lapsed, because no grace period applies to health policies
optionC: In force only for accidents until the premium is paid
optionD: In force, because the grace period is 10 days
explanation: Policies with monthly premiums have a 10-day grace period, so coverage continues through June 11 and any unpaid premium can be deducted from a claim. The 7-day grace period applies only to weekly premiums, and 31 days applies to other modes.

question: Jan's lapsed health policy is reinstated on the 45th day after her conditional receipt because the insurer never responded. Coverage for a new sickness begins:
explanation: If the insurer issues a conditional receipt and does not disapprove the application, the policy is reinstated on the 45th day. After reinstatement, accidents are covered immediately but sickness only if it begins more than 10 days later, which discourages reinstating after falling ill.

question: Under the uniform provisions, the normal deadlines for notice of claim, the insurer sending claim forms, and the insured filing proof of loss are:
explanation: The insured gives notice within 20 days of the loss, the insurer must furnish claim forms within 15 days of notice, and proof of loss is due within 90 days. If forms are not sent in time, the claimant may submit proof of loss in any written form.

question: Dave's medical claim is denied and he wants to sue his insurer. Under the legal actions provision, he may file suit:
optionA: Immediately, but within 1 year of the loss
optionB: Only after 90 days and within 2 years
optionC: Only after arbitration, with no time limit
optionD: From 60 days to 3 years after proof of loss
explanation: The insured must wait 60 days after filing proof of loss, giving the insurer time to investigate, and must sue within 3 years after proof of loss was required. Suing immediately is not allowed under this provision.

question: Four years after issue, an insurer learns that an applicant made an innocent misstatement on her health application. Under the time limit on certain defenses provision, the insurer:
optionA: May rescind the policy and refund premiums
optionB: May reduce benefits to match the true facts
optionC: Cannot void it or deny claims for it
optionD: May cancel the policy with 30 days' notice
explanation: Pennsylvania's time limit on certain defenses runs three years from the date of issue (Insurance Company Law section 618(A)(2)); after that, misstatements other than fraudulent ones cannot be used to void the policy or deny a claim. Four years have passed, so the insurer can neither rescind nor reduce benefits for the innocent misstatement.

question: An agent agrees in a letter to waive an exclusion on a client's individual health policy. Under the entire contract provision, the waiver is:
optionA: Valid, because the agent represents the insurer
optionB: Invalid unless an executive officer endorses it
optionC: Valid if the client signs the agent's letter
optionD: Invalid unless the state insurance department approves
explanation: The policy, endorsements and attached application form the entire contract, and only an executive officer of the insurer can approve a change, endorsed on the policy. Agents have no authority to change or waive policy provisions.

question: A clerk insured under an individual disability policy becomes a commercial roofer without telling the insurer, then is injured on a roof. The insurer will:
optionA: Pay what the premium buys at the roofer's rate
optionB: Deny the claim for failure to notify it
optionC: Pay the full benefit, then raise future premiums
optionD: Rescind the policy and refund all premiums
explanation: Under the change of occupation provision, a move to a more hazardous class reduces benefits to what the premium paid would buy at the new class. A move to a less hazardous occupation instead brings a lower rate and a refund of excess premium.

question: Paul stated his age as 40, but he was 45. He pays $300 a year; the correct premium at 45 is $400. His $2,000 monthly benefit becomes:
explanation: Benefits are adjusted to what the premium paid would have bought at the correct age: $300 / $400 = 75%, and 75% x $2,000 = $1,500. The insurer neither voids the policy nor keeps paying the full benefit.

question: Tom's employer has 75 employees. After Tom and his wife divorce, she may continue her coverage under his group health plan through COBRA for up to:
explanation: COBRA applies to employers with 20 or more employees and allows 36 months for divorce, death of the employee, Medicare entitlement or loss of dependent status. The 18-month period applies to termination or reduced hours, extended to 29 months for a disabled beneficiary, and a conversion policy may be available within 31 days after COBRA ends.

question: Which of the following is required of individual and group major medical plans under the Affordable Care Act?
optionA: Dependent coverage that ends at age 21
optionC: No lifetime limits on essential benefits
optionD: Medical underwriting to set each person's rate
explanation: The ACA bans annual and lifetime dollar limits on essential health benefits, requires guaranteed issue with no preexisting condition exclusions, and covers dependents to age 26. HIPAA, an earlier law, added portability protections and the privacy rule for health information.

question: Under Pennsylvania's time limit on certain defenses provision, non-fraudulent misstatements in the application can no longer void an individual health policy after:
explanation: Section 618(A)(2) of The Insurance Company Law sets the period at three years from the date of issue, longer than the two years in the NAIC model. After that only fraudulent misstatements can be used to void the policy or deny a claim.

question: An individual health policy has quarterly premiums. Pennsylvania requires a grace period of at least:
explanation: Section 618(A)(3) requires a grace period of at least 7 days for weekly premiums, 10 days for monthly premiums and 31 days for all other modes, so a quarterly policy gets 31 days.

question: A son disabled since age 10 is covered on his mother's individual health policy. He reaches the limiting age unmarried, unable to support himself and dependent on her. Coverage continues if she gives proof within:
explanation: Section 617(A)(9) keeps coverage in force for an unmarried child who became incapable of self-sustaining employment because of a disability before age 19 and is chiefly dependent on the policyholder, if proof is submitted within 31 days of reaching the limiting age.

question: Pennsylvania requires group health insurers to offer, at the policyholder's option, continued coverage of an employee's adult child through age 29 if the child:
optionA: Lives at home with a parent
explanation: Section 617.1 requires the option, at the employee's expense, for a child who is not married, has no dependents, is a Pennsylvania resident or full-time student, and has no other group, individual or government coverage. It applies to group policies, not individual ones.

question: An insured dies in an accident, and no beneficiary designation is in effect under his individual health policy. The accidental death benefit is paid to:
explanation: The payment of claims provision in section 618(A)(9) pays loss of life according to the beneficiary designation and, if none is then effective, to the insured's estate. All other benefits are payable to the insured.

question: Under the relation of earnings provision, the insurer compares disability benefits with the greater of earnings when disability began or average monthly earnings over the prior:
explanation: Section 618(B)(6) measures earnings as the greater of monthly earnings when the disability began or average monthly earnings for the two years before it. Benefits above that amount are reduced proportionately, with a refund of the excess premium.

question: Raj earns $6,000 a month. If an insurer limits disability income benefits to 60% of earnings, his maximum monthly benefit is:
explanation: 60% of $6,000 is $3,600. Insurers cap benefits below full earnings so the insured keeps an incentive to return to work, and $4,800 would be 80% of earnings.

question: After an illness, a sales manager returns to her job full time, but her income is 40% lower. Which benefit pays part of her lost income?
explanation: Residual disability benefits pay in proportion to the loss of income when the insured can still work but earns less. She is not totally disabled under either an own-occupation or any-occupation definition, and presumptive disability requires a severe loss such as sight, speech, hearing or two limbs.

question: A dentist who owns her practice becomes disabled. Which coverage pays her office rent, utilities and staff salaries, but not her own income?
explanation: Business overhead expense coverage reimburses the ongoing costs of running the business while the owner is disabled, but never the owner's salary. Its premiums are deductible as a business expense, so the benefits are taxable.

question: Sam's AD&D policy has a $100,000 principal sum. He loses one hand in a car accident. Under a typical policy, he receives:
explanation: The principal sum is paid for accidental death or the loss of two members, such as both hands or sight in both eyes. Loss of one member pays the capital sum, usually half the principal: $100,000 x 50% = $50,000.

question: Lisa's major medical plan has a $1,000 deductible and 80/20 coinsurance. She incurs $6,000 in covered charges. How much does Lisa pay?
explanation: Lisa pays the $1,000 deductible plus 20% of the remaining $5,000, which is $1,000, for a total of $2,000. Applying 20% to the full $6,000 on top of the deductible gives the wrong $2,200.

question: Joe's plan has a $500 deductible, 80/20 coinsurance and a $3,000 out-of-pocket maximum including the deductible. His covered bills total $40,000. Joe pays:
explanation: Without a cap, Joe would owe $500 plus 20% of $39,500, or $8,400. The stop-loss (out-of-pocket maximum) limits his total cost to $3,000, after which the plan pays 100%.

question: Nina's new dental plan covers cleanings right away but imposes a 12-month waiting period on crowns and bridges. These services fall into which category?
explanation: Dental plans group care as preventive (cleanings, exams), basic (fillings, extractions) and major (crowns, bridges, dentures), with major work carrying the longest waiting periods and paying the smallest percentage. Vision plans, a separate limited benefit, cover eye exams and lenses.

question: A new retiree wants a private plan that replaces Original Medicare Parts A and B and often includes drug coverage. She should choose:
optionA: Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage
optionC: A Medicare supplement Plan G policy
explanation: Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans are offered by private insurers in place of Parts A and B, often bundling Part D drug coverage. Part D covers only prescription drugs, and Medigap supplements Original Medicare rather than replacing it.

question: Ed spends 95 days in the hospital during one Medicare benefit period. Under Part A, days 91 through 95 are paid using:
optionC: Part B at 80% of the approved amount
optionD: Nothing, since Part A stops at day 60
explanation: Part A, premium-free with 40 quarters of coverage, pays days 1 to 60 after a deductible and days 61 to 90 with daily coinsurance in each benefit period, which ends after 60 days out of the hospital. Beyond day 90 the patient draws on 60 lifetime reserve days, which can be used only once.

question: Helen's assets exceed her state's Medicaid limit, so she pays her own nursing home bills until her assets fall below it. This process is called:
explanation: Medicaid is a needs-based program run by the states with federal funding, and spend-down is how applicants reduce assets or income to qualify. The 5-year look-back period instead reviews earlier asset transfers made to qualify.

question: Grace can still eat and use the toilet, but she now needs help bathing and dressing for the foreseeable future. Under a tax-qualified LTC policy, she:
optionA: Needs to lose 3 ADLs to qualify
optionB: Must first be hospitalized for 3 days
explanation: Tax-qualified LTC benefits begin when the insured cannot perform 2 of the 6 ADLs (bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, transferring, continence) for an expected 90 days or more, or has a severe cognitive impairment. Prior hospitalization cannot be required.

question: Ray needs help with bathing and dressing, provided by aides without medical training in an assisted living facility. This level of care is:
explanation: Custodial care helps with daily activities and can be given by people without medical training. Skilled care requires daily professional care ordered by a physician, intermediate care is occasional nursing, and respite care gives a family caregiver a break.

question: A Medigap insurer may not deny or price coverage based on health for an applicant who applies during the open enrollment period beginning with Part B enrollment, which lasts:
explanation: 31 Pa. Code 89.778(a) bars an issuer from denying, conditioning or pricing a Medicare supplement policy based on health for applications made before or during the 6-month period that begins the first day of the month the person enrolls in Part B.

question: A Pennsylvania Medicare supplement policy must let the buyer return it for a full premium refund within:
explanation: 31 Pa. Code 89.783 requires a notice on the first page that the policyholder may return the policy within 30 days of delivery and receive a premium refund. Ten days is the period for ordinary individual health policies.

question: A producer recommends a second Medicare supplement policy to a client who already has one. Under Pennsylvania rules this sale is:
explanation: 31 Pa. Code 89.787(b) prohibits any sale that would give an individual more than one Medicare supplement policy, and 89.787(a) requires the producer to make reasonable efforts to determine whether a purchase or replacement is appropriate.

question: A Pennsylvania long-term care policy must let the policyholder return it for a premium refund within:
explanation: Section 1110 of The Insurance Company Law gives individual long-term care policyholders, and group certificate holders who contribute to premium, the right to return the policy within 30 days of delivery for a refund.

question: A Pennsylvania long-term care policy may exclude a loss caused by a preexisting condition only if the loss begins within how long after coverage starts?
explanation: Section 1105(c) of The Insurance Company Law limits a preexisting condition to one treated or advised within six months before coverage and allows the exclusion only for a loss or confinement beginning within six months after the effective date.

question: When a producer solicits long-term care insurance, the outline of coverage must be delivered:
optionD: Only if the client requests it
explanation: Section 1111(c) requires an agent to deliver the outline of coverage before presenting an application or enrollment form; in direct response sales it must accompany the application. It summarizes benefits, exclusions, renewability and the right to return.

question: Which requirement for benefits is prohibited in a Pennsylvania long-term care policy?
optionD: Loss of two or more ADLs
explanation: Section 1108 of The Insurance Company Law bars conditioning eligibility on a prior stay in an institution, except for waiver of premium, postconfinement, postacute or recuperative benefits. Elimination periods and ADL or cognitive triggers are permitted.
